title: Jesus Begins His Public Work
overview: Mark opens at speed, moving from John the Baptist to Jesus' baptism, his first followers, and a rush of teaching and healing across Galilee.

parts.label: John prepares the way (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: Mark blends lines from Malachi and Isaiah to present John as the messenger sent ahead of the Lord's coming. John's rough clothes seem meant to recall the old prophet Elijah, and his washing in the river marked people turning their lives back to God.

parts.label: Baptism and testing (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: The torn sky, the dove and the voice mark Jesus out as God's beloved Son at the start of his work. Mark says little about the forty days of testing, and readers differ on what the number recalls, perhaps Israel's years in the wilderness or the forty days of Moses and Elijah.

parts.label: God's kingdom and four fishermen (vv. 14-20)
parts.note: Jesus announces that God's long awaited rule is arriving and calls people to turn around and trust this news. He invites four working fishermen to follow him, with a play on words: they will now gather people instead of fish.

parts.label: Authority in Capernaum (vv. 21-28)
parts.note: In the town's meeting house for prayer and Scripture, Jesus teaches on his own authority, not by citing earlier teachers as the experts in the law usually did. When a tormented man's spirit names him, Jesus silences it and drives it out, and the crowd links the teaching with the power.

parts.label: Healing crowds, a quiet dawn (vv. 29-39)
parts.note: After healing Simon's mother-in-law, Jesus is mobbed at sunset, when the day of rest ended and people could carry their sick to him. He silences the spirits, part of a puzzling pattern of secrecy in Mark whose purpose scholars still debate, then slips away to pray and moves on.

parts.label: A man with leprosy (vv. 40-45)
parts.note: This skin disease made a person ritually unclean and cut off from others, so Jesus' touch was startling. Ancient copies differ on whether he felt anger or pity, and he sends the man to the priest, whose approval would let him rejoin his community.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the kingdom of God that Jesus announces here is mainly a present reality, a future hope, or something already begun but not yet complete.
think: What do you think makes a person's words carry real authority, beyond their title or training?
